extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of literature and postcolonial/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ideological principles implied by Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's life and work for writers, teachers, and theatre practitioners working in (post)colonial contexts — especially regarding language choice, theatre practice, curriculum, and translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in native African languages / renounce colonial languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ wrote primarily in English before switching to writing primarily in Gikuyu and becoming a strong advocate for literature written in native African languages; Decolonising the Mind argues for African writers' expression in their native languages rather than European languages, in order to renounce lingering colonial ties and to build authentic African literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples on the page: renounce 'colonialist' names and linguistic practices; intentionally publish in Gikuyu (e.g., Devil on the Cross written in Gikuyu), and treat writing in indigenous languages as a political and cultural act to recover memory and authenticity. Anti-pattern: privileging European languages as the default literary medium, which Ngũgĩ characterises as continued colonial influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position African literature (including oral literature) at the centre of teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: While a professor at the University of Nairobi, Ngũgĩ argued that after the end of colonialism it was imperative that a university in Africa teach African literature, including oral literature, and do so with the realization of the richness of African languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: replace curricula that centre English literature with courses that prioritise African written and oral traditions. Example: the university dropped English Literature as a course of study and replaced it with one that positioned African literature at the centre. Anti-pattern: maintaining colonial curricula that marginalise indigenous literatures and oral forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demystify and liberate the theatrical process (spontaneity & audience participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1977 Ngũgĩ embarked upon a novel form of theatre in Kenya that sought to liberate the theatrical process from what he held to be 'the general bourgeois education system', by encouraging spontaneity and audience participation in the performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He sought to 'demystify' theatre and to avoid 'the process of alienation [that] produces a gallery of active stars and an undifferentiated mass of grateful admirers'. Practical guidance: design performances that are participatory, community-rooted, and that avoid star-focused hierarchies. Anti-pattern: theatre that reproduces passive spectatorship and elite theatrical distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literature and theatre as tools of political engagement and critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ's works (e.g., Petals of Blood, Ngaahika Ndeenda) carried strong political messages that challenged authoritarian power and colonial/neo-colonial structures, sometimes provoking severe state responses (e.g., shutdowns, imprisonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: accept political risk when work exposes injustice; aim for socially engaged narratives and plays that interrogate power. Example: Ngaahika Ndeenda's success and subsequent shutdown by the Kenyan regime; Ngũgĩ's imprisonment demonstrates potential consequences. Anti-pattern: producing politically neutral work that ignores social realities in contexts where literature can serve as critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate oral traditions, folklore, myth and epic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ argued for valuing oral literature and used folk material in his works (e.g., Matigari based on a Gikuyu folk tale; The Perfect Nine reimagines an origin story in epic verse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: draw on oral storytelling techniques, mythic structures, and communal narratives to create works that resonate culturally. Example: The Perfect Nine as a quest novel-in-verse that fuses folklore and feminist/pan-African perspectives. Anti-pattern: dismissing oral forms as non-literary or subordinate to European literary models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and translation activism to broaden reach and recover languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ's short story 'The Upright Revolution' was translated into more than 100 languages; he also translated his own works into English. He engaged with translation projects to circulate African-language literature widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: actively translate indigenous-language works (including self-translation) and participate in translation initiatives to increase accessibility and cross-cultural exchange. Example: being both author and translator for The Perfect Nine and longlisting for International Booker. Anti-pattern: leaving indigenous-language works untranslated and thus limiting reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with urgency and connect to readers' lived experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ cited George Lamming's influence — that a novel 'could be made to speak to me, could, with a compelling urgency, touch cords deep down in me' — implying a standard that literature should speak directly and urgently to readers' realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: craft narratives that evoke emotional and political immediacy and that relate to readers' historical and material circumstances. Anti-pattern: producing detached or purely aestheticised work that fails to engage readerly concerns or social context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community-based cultural institutions and education as part of literary practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ helped establish the Kamiriithu Community Education and Cultural Centre to organise African Theatre and community cultural activity, integrating education and performance as part of cultural production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: situate creative practice within community education projects and cultural centres to foster participatory arts and local ownership. Example: Kamiriithu's role in staging Ngaahika Ndeenda. Anti-pattern: isolating literary production from community engagement and popular education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt decolonial personal/practical stances (name, identity, material practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ngũgĩ renounced the Anglicised name 'James Ngugi' as 'colonialist' and changed his name to Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o; he also continued practices like writing in Gikuyu under adverse conditions (e.g., composing Devil on the Cross on prison-issued toilet paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: consider the symbolic and material choices (names, language, modes of production) as part of decolonial practice in literature. Examples show both symbolic (name change) and practical (writing in prison) acts. Anti-pattern: treating such choices as irrelevant personal matters rather than politically significant acts.
